nodes.title: Identity providers and federation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.

questions.q: A multinational firm is consolidating identity onto a single cloud IdP and wants every workforce login, including for legacy on-prem apps that only speak Kerberos or header-based auth, to be brokered through that IdP with conditional access and continuous evaluation. Which architectural pattern fits best?
choices: Deploy an identity-aware proxy (IAP) in front of the legacy apps and federate the IdP via SAML/OIDC to the proxy
Synchronise password hashes from the IdP into the legacy directories so each app authenticates locally
Publish the legacy apps to the internet behind a CDN-based WAF with IP allow-listing for corporate ranges
Distribute long-lived service-account credentials to users and rotate them via a password vault
questions.explanation: An identity-aware proxy sits in front of the legacy app and terminates the user session with the modern IdP over SAML/OIDC, then injects the Kerberos ticket or auth header downstream. This brings the legacy app under conditional access and continuous evaluation without rewriting it. Synchronising hashes leaves each app authenticating locally and bypasses central policy, a WAF with allow-listing enforces network rules but not user identity, and shared service accounts violate non-repudiation.

questions.q: An architect is asked to make the firm "crypto-agile" ahead of NIST's post-quantum migration. Which design choice most directly enables a future swap from RSA-2048 to a PQC algorithm like ML-KEM without re-architecting applications?
choices: Pin a single cipher suite in every application's TLS config so behaviour is predictable
Centralise key operations behind an abstraction (KMS or PKCS#11) and reference keys by identifier, not algorithm
Increase RSA key length to 4096 bits across the estate
Ship private keys inside each application container so rotation is independent
questions.explanation: Crypto-agility means applications call a key by identifier ("signing-key-prod") through a KMS or PKCS#11 abstraction; the algorithm behind that identifier can be swapped from RSA to ML-KEM/ML-DSA with no application code change. Pinning a suite blocks future migration, larger RSA keys do not address Shor's-algorithm exposure, and embedding private keys in containers makes rotation harder and widens blast radius.

questions.q: During threat modelling of a new payments microservice, the team is using STRIDE. A reviewer flags that an attacker who tampers with a message between the API gateway and the ledger could silently rewrite the amount. Which control category most directly addresses this STRIDE element?
choices: Rate limiting at the gateway to throttle abuse
Message-level signing (e.g., HMAC or JWS) verified by the ledger
TLS 1.3 between gateway and ledger only
Output encoding on the customer-facing API
questions.explanation: STRIDE's T is Tampering; the canonical mitigation is integrity at the message layer — HMAC or JWS — verified end-to-end so even a compromised intermediary cannot rewrite the amount. TLS 1.3 only protects the transport hop and trusts every node in the chain, rate limiting addresses denial-of-service rather than integrity, and output encoding mitigates XSS at the browser edge, not server-to-server tampering.

questions.q: A regulator now requires the firm to produce a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for every shipped artefact and to respond to new CVEs within 72 hours. Which pipeline change most efficiently meets both obligations?
choices: Generate a CycloneDX SBOM at build time, store it with the artefact, and re-scan stored SBOMs continuously against an updated vulnerability feed
Have each application team run a manual `pip list` quarterly and email the result to compliance
Block all open-source dependencies and rewrite functionality in-house
Replace SCA tooling with a network IDS to detect exploitation after release
questions.explanation: A build-time CycloneDX (or SPDX) SBOM gives a fixed inventory tied to each artefact; continuously re-scanning that stored SBOM against an updated CVE feed surfaces new vulnerabilities without needing to rebuild, which is exactly what a 72-hour response window demands. Manual quarterly lists cannot meet a 72-hour SLA, banning open-source is operationally infeasible, and an IDS detects exploitation after the fact rather than identifying vulnerable components.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A bank is re-issuing its internal PKI. Auditors require that the root CA's private key cannot be exported, even by administrators, and that any signing event is independently logged. Which design satisfies both constraints?
flashcards.back: A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM keeps the private key non-exportable in hardware, and the documented key ceremony with M-of-N quorum plus tamper-evident logs provides the independent record auditors expect. A PFX file is exportable by anyone holding the passphrase, co-locating the root with the subordinate negates the offline-root model, and tying the key to a single AD account creates a personal single point of failure with no separation of duties.

flashcards.front: The SOC is buried in low-fidelity SIEM alerts and wants to bring mean-time-to-respond down without hiring more analysts. Which capability most directly addresses the volume problem?
flashcards.back: SOAR is the layer designed to triage and contain SIEM cases automatically: it enriches with threat intel, executes containment playbooks (disable account, isolate host) and only escalates the residual to a human. Running two SIEMs doubles work without reducing it, swapping EDR taxonomies does not reduce alert volume, and outsourcing transfers the problem but does not solve fidelity.

flashcards.front: During a tabletop, the IR lead notes that the firm's BC/DR plan promises a four-hour RTO but the database is asynchronously replicated to the DR region with a 30-minute lag. Which gap does this most directly create?
flashcards.back: RTO is how fast you can be back; RPO is how much data you can afford to lose. A 30-minute async lag locks the firm into at least a 30-minute RPO regardless of how quickly DR is brought up, so the gap is between the business's accepted data-loss tolerance and what the architecture actually delivers. Bandwidth, change-management and dual-control may all need work but are not what this specific lag exposes.

flashcards.front: A SaaS vendor proposes inline access to customer email for spam classification. The CISO must approve based on the firm's data-classification policy. Which control combination is the minimum acceptable safeguard for processing data marked Confidential?
flashcards.back: For Confidential processing the firm needs contractual coverage (DPA), key control so the vendor cannot read data without the firm's key (BYOK / customer-managed keys), and independent assurance that the vendor's controls actually operate — a SOC 2 Type II covering Security/Confidentiality. "Act reasonably" is unenforceable, ISO 9001 is a quality standard with no security scope, and a firewall rule does nothing about what the vendor does with the data once it arrives.

questions.q: A bank is re-issuing its internal PKI. Auditors require that the root CA's private key cannot be exported, even by administrators, and that any signing event is independently logged. Which design satisfies both constraints?
choices: Generate the root key in a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM, keep it offline, and require dual-control ceremony with tamper-evident logs
Store the root key in a password-protected PFX file on an air-gapped laptop accessed by a single admin
Hold the root key in the same online subordinate CA database so issuance is automated
Encrypt the root key with the domain administrator's AD credentials
questions.explanation: A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM keeps the private key non-exportable in hardware, and the documented key ceremony with M-of-N quorum plus tamper-evident logs provides the independent record auditors expect. A PFX file is exportable by anyone holding the passphrase, co-locating the root with the subordinate negates the offline-root model, and tying the key to a single AD account creates a personal single point of failure with no separation of duties.

questions.q: The SOC is buried in low-fidelity SIEM alerts and wants to bring mean-time-to-respond down without hiring more analysts. Which capability most directly addresses the volume problem?
choices: A SOAR platform that runs enrichment and containment playbooks against SIEM cases
A second SIEM running in parallel for cross-validation
Switching the EDR vendor to one with a different alert taxonomy
Outsourcing the SOC entirely to a managed provider
questions.explanation: SOAR is the layer designed to triage and contain SIEM cases automatically: it enriches with threat intel, executes containment playbooks (disable account, isolate host) and only escalates the residual to a human. Running two SIEMs doubles work without reducing it, swapping EDR taxonomies does not reduce alert volume, and outsourcing transfers the problem but does not solve fidelity.

questions.q: During a tabletop, the IR lead notes that the firm's BC/DR plan promises a four-hour RTO but the database is asynchronously replicated to the DR region with a 30-minute lag. Which gap does this most directly create?
choices: An RPO larger than the business has actually accepted
A bandwidth ceiling on the production link
A failure of the change-management process
A breakdown of dual-control on backup tapes
questions.explanation: RTO is how fast you can be back; RPO is how much data you can afford to lose. A 30-minute async lag locks the firm into at least a 30-minute RPO regardless of how quickly DR is brought up, so the gap is between the business's accepted data-loss tolerance and what the architecture actually delivers. Bandwidth, change-management and dual-control may all need work but are not what this specific lag exposes.

questions.q: A SaaS vendor proposes inline access to customer email for spam classification. The CISO must approve based on the firm's data-classification policy. Which control combination is the minimum acceptable safeguard for processing data marked Confidential?
choices: A signed contract clause stating the vendor will "act reasonably" with the data
A signed DPA, tenant-scoped encryption keys held by the customer (BYOK), and a SOC 2 Type II report covering the relevant criteria
A vendor self-attestation that they are ISO 9001 certified
A network firewall rule restricting the vendor's source IPs
questions.explanation: For Confidential processing the firm needs contractual coverage (DPA), key control so the vendor cannot read data without the firm's key (BYOK / customer-managed keys), and independent assurance that the vendor's controls actually operate — a SOC 2 Type II covering Security/Confidentiality. "Act reasonably" is unenforceable, ISO 9001 is a quality standard with no security scope, and a firewall rule does nothing about what the vendor does with the data once it arrives.

nodes.title: Cloud security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud security adapts classic CIA-triad defenses to a model where the provider runs the infrastructure and you secure your data, identities, and configurations on top of it. Exams test the shared responsibility split, identity-based access control, encryption, and the misconfigurations (like public storage buckets) that cause most real breaches.

flashcards.front: What does the shared responsibility model define?
flashcards.back: It splits security duties between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider secures the underlying infrastructure (the cloud itself); the customer secures what they put in it — data, identities, OS/app config, and access controls. The exact line shifts with the service model (IaaS gives you more responsibility than SaaS).

A Cloud Access Security Broker — a policy enforcement point that sits between users and cloud services. It gives visibility into cloud usage (including unsanctioned shadow IT), enforces access and DLP policies, and applies threat protection across multiple cloud apps from one control plane.

flashcards.front: Encryption in transit vs at rest — what protects what?
flashcards.back: In transit protects data moving over networks, typically with TLS, so it can't be read if intercepted. At rest protects stored data on disks/objects/databases via encryption keys, so stolen media or storage is unreadable. Strong posture uses both, ideally with customer-managed keys.

flashcards.front: Why are public storage buckets a top cloud misconfiguration?
flashcards.back: A bucket or blob container left open to anonymous/public read exposes data to the entire internet with no exploit required. It's a default-and-forget mistake; the fix is least-privilege IAM policies, blocking public access at the account level, and continuous config scanning.

questions.q: An architect is designing a Zero Trust deployment for a hybrid workforce. Which signal source should drive continuous access decisions, in addition to user identity?
choices: Device posture (compliance, EDR health, patch level) evaluated at each request
The user's office floor number recorded in HR
Whether the user is connected to the corporate Wi-Fi SSID
The colour of the badge issued at hiring
questions.explanation: Zero Trust replaces the network-perimeter assumption with continuous evaluation of identity plus device posture — is the endpoint compliant, is EDR healthy, are patches current — re-checked at each request rather than at login. SSID and HR floor data are network/location proxies that Zero Trust explicitly distrusts, and badge colour is not a runtime authorisation signal.

questions.q: A DLP rollout keeps blocking legitimate finance traffic because executives mail spreadsheets containing what the engine classifies as PAN-like strings. Which tuning step preserves protection while reducing false positives?
choices: Disable the DLP module for the finance department
Combine the regex with a Luhn check and require a second proximity keyword (e.g., "card", "CVV") before flagging
Lower the DLP confidence threshold so more events fire
Move the DLP enforcement point downstream of the mail relay so it sees fewer messages
questions.explanation: Validated detectors layer a Luhn check (real PANs satisfy the checksum, random 16-digit numbers do not) and a proximity keyword to cut the false positives without lowering protection. Disabling DLP for finance throws the policy away exactly where the sensitive data lives, lowering the threshold makes false positives worse, and moving enforcement downstream just changes when the same noise arrives.

questions.q: An attacker exploits an SSRF in a public web app to reach the cloud instance metadata service and steal a long-lived IAM role credential. Which preventive control would have most directly blocked the credential theft?
choices: Disable IPv6 on the workload subnet
Enforce IMDSv2 (session-token-required metadata) so the SSRF cannot read role credentials with a simple GET
Apply a rate limit on the application's egress
Run weekly password rotation on the root account
questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a PUT to obtain a short-lived session token before any metadata GET succeeds; a typical SSRF that only issues GETs cannot satisfy that handshake and so cannot fetch the role credentials. Disabling IPv6 does not affect the IPv4 link-local metadata endpoint, egress rate limiting does not stop a single small request, and rotating the root password is unrelated to instance-role credential exposure.

questions.q: Forensic responders arrive at a compromised Linux host that is still powered on. Which collection order best preserves evidentiary value?
choices: Pull the power cable first, then image the disk
Capture volatile memory and network state first (RAM, /proc, netstat), then a forensic disk image, then power down
Run anti-virus to clean the host before any imaging so the system is safe to keep online
Reboot into single-user mode and copy /var/log out
questions.explanation: RFC 3227's order-of-volatility says capture the most ephemeral data first: RAM, running processes, open sockets, then non-volatile disk imaging, then shut down. Pulling power destroys volatile evidence, running AV alters timestamps and may delete attacker artefacts, and rebooting clears RAM and may trigger anti-forensics in init scripts.
